props.title: Possessed
props.initialSlug: Nun's dark obsession leads to murder & madness

sections.content: Possessed (1947) stands as one of film noir's most haunting psychological thrillers, with Joan Crawford delivering a tour-de-force performance as Louise Howell, a mentally unstable woman whose obsessive love drives her to madness. The film opens with a masterful sequence - Crawford wandering the streets of Los Angeles in a dissociative state, establishing the fractured psychological state that defines the narrative. Director Curtis Bernhardt employs German Expressionist techniques similar to those in The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920), using distorted angles and shadow play to visualize Louise's deteriorating mental state.

sections.content: The film's exploration of mental illness was groundbreaking for 1947, predating more famous psychological noirs like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Sudden Fear (1952). Crawford's Louise represents a departure from typical femme fatale characters - instead of calculated manipulation, we see genuine psychological deterioration. The film's flashback structure, starting with Louise in a catatonic state and gradually revealing how she got there, influenced later psychological thrillers like Spellbound (1945) and The Snake Pit (1948).

Cinematographer Joseph Valentine's work deserves special attention, particularly in scenes depicting Louise's hallucinations. His techniques would influence later films about mental illness, including Shock Corridor (1963) and Repulsion (1965). The film's approach to psychiatric treatment, while dated, was relatively progressive for its time, showing mental illness as a medical condition rather than moral failing. sections.content: Possessed helped establish a subgenre of female-centered psychological thrillers that would flourish in the 1950s and beyond. Films like Lizzie (1957) and Three Faces of Eve (1957) followed its lead in exploring women's mental health struggles, while later works like Images (1972) and Repulsion (1965) built upon its visual representation of psychological disturbance. Crawford's performance set a benchmark for depicting mental illness on screen, influencing later acclaimed portrayals in films like A Woman Under the Influence (1974).
